claims.text: Adding 10 vol% SiC whiskers and spark-plasma sintering at 1500 °C will enable full densification of ZrB2.
A transient B2O3-SiO2 liquid film will form at ZrB2 grain boundaries during sintering.
The transient B2O3-SiO2 liquid film will lower the temperature required for densification through liquid-phase sintering.
The SiC whiskers will form an interconnected network in the sintered body.
During high-temperature exposure, SiC whiskers will oxidize to form a continuous SiO2 scale.
The SiO2 scale will slow further oxidation of the composite.
The SiO2 scale will block molten-aluminum infiltration.
SiC whiskers will bridge cracks and thereby increase fracture toughness.
The composite will reach at least 98% of theoretical density.
The composite will exhibit at least a 30% increase in fracture toughness.
Oxidation weight gain will be below 2 mg/cm² after 100 h in air at 1500 °C.
Mass loss will be below 1% after 100 h in molten aluminum at 700 °C.
Pure ZrB2 sintered at 2300 °C has approximately 95% theoretical density.
Under the stated oxidation test, pure ZrB2 will gain more than 5 mg/cm².
Under the stated molten-aluminum test, pure ZrB2 will lose more than 10% of its mass.
The SiC-whisker composite will have greater toughness, lower oxidation rate, and better molten-metal corrosion resistance than both ZrB2 prepared at 2300 °C and prior lower-temperature specimens.
The proposed composite is applicable with 8–12 vol% whiskers, sintering at 1400–1600 °C, service temperatures up to 1600 °C, and molten-aluminum temperatures of 700–750 °C.

contradictions.description: The prediction requires at least 98% density, but the experiment only falsifies the hypothesis below 95%; a result from 95% to under 98% would violate the prediction without falsifying it.

The prediction requires at least a 30% toughness increase, but the hypothesis is only falsified below a 10% increase; results from 10% to under 30% are inconsistent with the prediction yet pass the falsification rule.
The predicted oxidation gain is below 2 mg/cm², whereas falsification requires a gain above 4 mg/cm²; intermediate results fail the stated prediction without falsifying the hypothesis.
The predicted molten-aluminum mass loss is below 1%, whereas falsification requires loss above 5%; intermediate losses fail the prediction without triggering falsification.
The hypothesis claims superiority over prior lower-temperature specimens, but the experiment includes only a 2300 °C pure-ZrB2 control and therefore cannot evaluate that comparison.
